scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
Dr. Blaine Fisher is the founder and CEO of Rocketproof.ai, an instructional technology leader, professor, and interdisciplinary scholar at Tulane University whose work spans artificial intelligence, education, technology ethics, emergency management, geospatial science, and archaeology.

At Tulane, Dr. Fisher serves as a Senior Instructional Technology Specialist and plays a central role in supporting the university’s educational technology ecosystem. He administers the Canvas Learning Management System, leads initiatives through the Innovative Learning Center, and develops faculty training across artificial intelligence, Canvas, YuJa, Top Hat, Qualtrics, Box, Microsoft Teams, Zoom, and other emerging technologies. He has trained more than 2,000 faculty members, with a particular focus on practical AI literacy, instructional design, and preparing teaching and assessment for an AI-rich academic environment.

Dr. Fisher is also an active AI educator and consultant. He has developed and delivered AI bootcamps and professional development programs for university faculty, staff, community audiences, international groups, and executive learners, including programs in Dubai. His teaching and workshops cover topics such as AI fundamentals, applied artificial intelligence, AI for research, AI-enhanced course design, AI as a second brain, AI productivity, agentic AI, and responsible AI use.

As a professor at Tulane’s School of Professional Advancement, Dr. Fisher teaches undergraduate and graduate courses across a range of disciplines, including AI in Modern Society, Applied Artificial Intelligence, The Ethics of Technology Through Science Fiction, Health and Medical Issues in Emergency Management, UI/UX Design, Enterprise Applications Architecture, and geospatial science and GIS applications.

His interest in the future of assessment led him to create Rocketproof.ai, an AI-powered authentic assessment platform designed for the generative AI era. Rocketproof helps educators evaluate the understanding, reasoning, and communication behind student work by pairing submitted assignments with structured oral defenses. The project reflects a broader focus in Dr. Fisher’s work on AI literacy, communication skills, academic judgment, and the redesign of teaching practices as generative AI changes how students create and interact with academic work.

Dr. Fisher holds a Ph.D. in Geography and Anthropology from Louisiana State University, with a specialization in Maya archaeology. His interdisciplinary background also includes nearly a decade of experience as a paramedic and flight paramedic, leadership in environmental health and safety programs, and ongoing work as a remote sensing and geospatial scientist supporting coastal resilience and wetlands research through drones, LiDAR, GIS, and spatial data analysis. He also remains active in archaeological research at ancient Maya sites.

Dr. Fisher is a recipient of the John Percy Dyer Award for Teaching Excellence and has served as a Faculty Fellow with Tulane’s School of Professional Advancement and Newcomb College Institute. Across his teaching, research, technology leadership, and work with Rocketproof.ai, his central focus is helping people understand how emerging technologies can be used thoughtfully while preserving human judgment, communication, and meaningful evidence of learning.

title.rendered: The Message Runner: What Tech can Learn from the Creative Practices of Theater, Film, and TV. by Dan Woods

content.rendered: Sidney Lumet said the job of a director is to make sure everyone is making the same movie. Sadly in the world of tech nobody plays the role of the director who creates and documenting the vision and message, teaches it to everyone in ways they can understand it, collaborates and rehearses to make it better, takes it on an out of town tryout, and improves it as more is understood. Dan Woods has created vision and a process for a role called the Message Runner, what the director role should be in the world of tech. The Message Runner vision is inspired by Stanislavsky’s practices for training actors for roles, existing frameworks for directors, critics like Eric Bentley, drama teachers like Kenneth Rowe, and the ways that television showrunners adapt from episode to episode. This vision is adapted to the reality of a tech company and is enhanced with practices like Jobs To Be Done and new framework for evaluating product market fit. Finally, the vision relies on a normalized form of messaging expressed in a semantic model that allows AI to be applied it various ways to analysis of a company, competitors, and a category. Once the Message Runner idea take hold of your mind, you won’t make the same common mistakes ever again.

title.rendered: Coding for Good at AI Speed: Mapping New Orleans’ Bumpy Roads by Adam Davies

content.rendered:
Two years ago I shelved an idea because the research paper had too much math in it. This spring I built it over a long weekend.

Bumpy Roads turns the phone on your handlebars into a road-quality scanner. Accelerometer data is just a signal. Filter it right and it becomes a roughness score, and that score becomes a color-coded map of which New Orleans side streets are actually rideable. Volunteers mapping quiet bike routes across the city now use it to settle arguments that used to be pure opinion.

I’ll walk the whole loop: problem -> dumb first algorithm -> a deployed app running on my own box -> real rides that broke it → using academic papers to improve it. Claude did the parts I couldn’t, like a 1960s speech-compression algorithm I’d never heard of. I did the parts it couldn’t, like riding around finding out where it was wrong.

I’ll close on how to find the version of this in your own neighborhood – the problem you actually want to solve.

title.rendered: Beyond Hallucination: Verifying AI Results for Accessible Digital Experiences by Mingren (Michael) Fu

content.rendered: AI can help us understand information, summarize content, create digital experiences, act on our behalf, and so much more. As the role of AI continues to evolve, how can we use AI effectively while ensuring the results promote equal access? This session introduces ACCESS, a practical framework for evaluating AI results through a digital accessibility lens. Through rapid, real-world examples, attendees will learn to identify potential gaps in AI results, verify those results against key criteria, and assess whether all users have equal access to essential information and opportunities.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
Mingren (Michael) Fu is a CPACC-certified Digital Accessibility Specialist at the University of Illinois Chicago, dedicated to creating inclusive and accessible digital experiences. With expertise in WCAG compliance, UX/UI design, and assistive technologies, he helps organizations identify and remove accessibility barriers to ensure usability for all. 

Michael has advanced accessibility initiatives at New York University and led research and design projects for the United Nations, Google, and the Humboldt Forum Museum, applying human-centered design and compliance strategies to improve digital inclusivity. As a problem solver and AI enthusiast, he is passionate about bridging technology and accessibility to drive innovative and equitable solutions.

title.rendered: Nobody Trains You for This: Junior Talent, AI, and the Job Market by Johnnie James II

content.rendered:
Nobody trains you for this.

Junior developers are entering a job market that demands experience they cannot have and skills no one taught them. The industry wants AI-ready talent, but the entry level is moving faster than the training.

This panel brings together Operation Spark alumni who are navigating that gap. No sugarcoating. No recruitment pitches. Just a conversation about what happens when the training pipeline meets a market that has changed underneath it.

We will talk about:

– What junior devs are actually being asked to know?
– Where they are finding (and not finding) opportunities?
– How AI is reshaping the skills gap?
– Who is responsible for building the bridge from skill attainment to job attainment?

scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
Johnnie James II is an entrepreneur, sustAInability advocate, and CEO of PoH Farms, bringing REEFBUDS® — a patented plant-based artificial reef system with over twenty years of successful field deployment in the Philippines — to the U.S. Gulf Coast. He is the creator of Mardi Bar Wars, a community recycling initiative that diverted over 41,000 pounds of glass from New Orleans landfills during its Mardi Gras 2025 pilot. 

A New Orleanian now based in Baton Rouge, Johnnie serves as Operations Coordinator at Operation Spark, a nonprofit software training program with a 90%+ job placement rate. His work has been recognized with NOLAvate Black’s Tech 30 “Black Excellence Award.” Johnnie is a disciple, husband, father, poet, and servant leader committed to building regenerative economies and resilient communities. Learn more at OperationSpark.org and REEFBUDS.com.

title.rendered: A Four Horsemen of Sustainable Innovation? by Johnnie James II

content.rendered:
The four tracks of this conference — Open Source, Biz Dev, Accessibility, and Analog Arts — are not necessarily separate conversations. They are interdependent forces that, if aligned, can drive sustainable innovation. If left unaligned, could they work against a sustAInable future?

This panel explores how a small team is working to bring these domains together using a real-world case study: Biomimicrete™ a biomimetic concrete material platform for carbon sequestration, coastal protection, and restoration. Attendees will leave with a framework for applying the same logic to their own work.

title.rendered: Artificial Intelligence, Gaussian Splatting, and the Future of Visual Effects: Lessons from the Production of Cyberpunk Manifesto by Trai Thomas

content.rendered:
Presenter: Dr. Trai Thomas

Presentation Title: Artificial Intelligence, Gaussian Splatting, and the Future of Visual Effects: Lessons from the Production of Cyberpunk Manifesto

Presentation Overview

This presentation examines the growing role of artificial intelligence in contemporary film production and explores how emerging technologies such as Gaussian Splatting and real-time rendering engines are transforming the visual effects industry. Drawing from firsthand experience producing the narrative feature film Cyberpunk Manifesto, Dr. Trai Thomas will discuss how AI-generated animation and image synthesis tools were utilized in place of portions of a traditional visual effects pipeline to create cinematic sequences more efficiently and cost-effectively.

The presentation will explore the advantages and limitations of AI-assisted production workflows, including reductions in production costs, accelerated development timelines, and increased accessibility for independent filmmakers. Particular attention will be given to the potential of Gaussian Splatting technologies and their integration with platforms such as Unreal Engine, which may significantly alter the way digital environments, visual effects, and virtual productions are created in the coming decade.

Objectives

Participants will:

Gain an understanding of how artificial intelligence is currently being integrated into film production workflows.
Learn how AI-generated animation and imagery were utilized during the production of Cyberpunk Manifesto.
Explore the emerging role of Gaussian Splatting as an alternative or supplement to traditional 3D modeling and visual effects techniques.
Examine the relationship between AI technologies and real-time rendering platforms such as Unreal Engine.
Discuss how these technologies may democratize filmmaking by lowering barriers to entry for independent creators.
Consider the ethical, creative, and professional implications of AI’s growing influence on the film and media industries.
Relevance

As artificial intelligence continues to disrupt creative industries, filmmakers, designers, educators, and digital media professionals are increasingly seeking to understand both the opportunities and challenges presented by these technologies. This presentation offers a practical case study from an independent feature film production while providing a forward-looking discussion about the future of visual effects, virtual production, and digital storytelling.

Presenter Biography

Dr. Trai Thomas is a filmmaker, marketing professional, and cultural preservation scholar based in New Orleans, Louisiana. He recently completed his debut narrative feature film, Cyberpunk Manifesto, which incorporated artificial intelligence-generated animation and visual effects technologies as part of its production process. Dr. Thomas holds a Doctor of Design degree with a concentration in cultural preservation and museum studies and is passionate about exploring the intersection of emerging technology, media production, and storytelling.

Presentation Format
Presentation Length: 15 – 30 minutes
Audience: Filmmakers, media professionals, students, educators, digital artists, and technology enthusiasts
Includes: Lecture presentation, visual demonstrations, production case studies, and audience Q&A session

scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
Dr. Trai Thomas recently completed his debut narrative feature film, Cyberpunk Manifesto, utilizing artificial intelligence to create the film’s animated sequences in place of a traditional visual effects pipeline. Drawing on emerging AI-driven technologies, the production explored new methods of digital storytelling that significantly reduced both production costs and development time while expanding creative possibilities for independent filmmakers.

Thomas believes that, in the coming years, technologies such as Gaussian Splatting and other real-time rendering systems may increasingly challenge traditional VFX workflows that rely on complex modeling, animation, and compositing pipelines. When combined with platforms such as Unreal Engine, these tools have the potential to make high-quality visual effects more accessible to independent creators by reducing technical barriers, streamlining production processes, and lowering overall costs.

According to Thomas, the growing adoption of AI-assisted workflows represents a significant shift in the film industry, enabling smaller productions to achieve visual results that were previously attainable only through large teams and substantial budgets. He views these developments not as a replacement for artists, but as new creative tools that can democratize filmmaking and expand opportunities for emerging storytellers.

Build your own AI agent without cloud costs or privacy tradeoffs. In this hands-on crash course, we’ll walk through spinning up a fully functional agentic AI system on your laptop using open source tools and freely available models.

Walk away with a working agent setup you can extend with your own tools and data—no vendor lock-in, no recurring API bills, full control over your data.

content.rendered:
Get hands on with the first 3 layers of the electrotech stack (lithium-ion batteries, electromagnetic motors, power electronics) by converting an analog bike to electric and back as fast as possible.

Talk about the other two layers (embedded compute, llms/world models) while we build.

Walk out with deeper energy intuition, ways to get involved in the energy transition in nola.

title.rendered: The Most Valuable AI Skill Is Saying No : Screening AI use cases for real return. by Dustin T Hughes

content.rendered:
Your best AI idea is probably wrong. The boring one you didn’t pitch is probably worth thousands.

This is a 90 minute sorting exercise for people done with demos. You’ll inventory two weeks of your real work, push three candidates through a four-gate screen, and let the math pick, not the hype. Then you build the winner right there and watch the minutes come back.

Most sessions promise what AI can do. This one shows you what yours should.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio: Dustin Hughes is VP of Technology at Laborde Products, a marine diesel distributor, where he leads a small technology team supporting 95 people across three locations. Much of his recent work has been practical AI adoption: helping everyone from executives to service techs and parts counter staff find the places where AI genuinely saves time, and being honest about the places where it doesn’t. He currently leads Waypoint, Laborde’s company-wide AI program, built on a simple standard: a win only counts with the task, the prompt, the output, and the time saved. He’s been building software for 25 years and working with AI since 2013.

title.rendered: AI Resume Matching Service by Mason Mitchell

content.rendered: I’m am using this presentation to bring awareness to ways AI can be implementing in opportunity seeking, specifically in the realms of fellowship, internship, and research, where the rise of ATS AI has made resume curation and matching increasingly important for putting ourselves in the best position, both as recruiter and recruit.

title.rendered: Life’s a Pitch: THE SCIENCE OF GETTING PEOPLE TO LISTEN TO, TRUST IN, AND SAY “YES” TO YOUR IDEAS. by Tom Martin

content.rendered: Most presentations fail before anyone opens PowerPoint, because the fix people reach for is better delivery, not better design. This session uses neuroscience, behavioral psychology, and cognitive load theory to explain why audiences tune out and how to structure a presentation that holds attention and drives action. Bring a real presentation. Leave with a plan to rebuild it.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio: Tom Martin is the founder and president of Converse Digital, an agency business development consulting firm based in New Orleans. He is the author of The Invisible Sale and creator of the Propinquity Principle, the framework underpinning his consulting practice. A veteran of agency new business dating back to the 1990s, Tom ran two agencies before pivoting full time to consulting in 2022. He is a keynote speaker whose signature talk, Life’s a Pitch, draws on decades spent pitching, presenting, and closing high stakes deals.

title.rendered: Intro to Clown by Grace Bertuccelli-Booth

content.rendered: Connect with your audience and find your funny! This introduction to theatrical clown includes games and exercises geared towards accessing onstage vulnerability, responsiveness, and your own personal brand of clown humor. We’ll explore entrances and exits, audience relationship, character improvisation, and red-nose clown as the building blocks for your own unique clown characters.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio: Grace Bertuccelli-Booth is a performer, director, and teacher based in New Orleans, LA. She holds an M.F.A. in Ensemble-Based Physical Theatre from Dell’Arte International and a B.A. in Theatre & Dance from Amherst College. Her performance creations and pedagogy center around mask-work, informed by training in Clown, Commedia Dell’Arte, the Greek chorus, and studies in Balinese mask-carving.  Grace is focused on the intersection of performance and health advocacy.  She works as a Healthcare Clown with Prescription Joy and is a co-author of “Jane Doe in Wonderland,” a survivor-centered project preventing human trafficking through community awareness.  Grace is also a collaborating artist with Uplift Physical Theatre. More info at www.graceboothperformance.com.

title.rendered: The Intentional Page: A Device-Free Writing Lab with S.I.L.K. by Marcus Rosser and Kaylon Seaberry (S.I.L.K.)

content.rendered: Before a writer chooses a tool, they choose what they mean. Co-facilitated by Marcus Rosser and Kaylon Seaberry, known as S.I.L.K., this device-free lab uses observation, memory, constraint, and revision to help participants turn lived experience into intentional writing. Through short exercises, paired feedback, and an optional final reading, each participant leaves with a finished micro-piece and a repeatable method for making language more specific, personal, and alive. No AI, screens, or prior writing experience required.

title.rendered: Beyond Chatbots: Turn One SOP into a Working AI Workflow by Marcus Rosser

content.rendered: Most organizations do not need another chatbot—they need one repeatable process that saves time without surrendering control. Using a real small-organization workflow, Marcus Rosser demonstrates how to turn an SOP into an AI-assisted system using task decomposition, reusable skills, tool routing, human approvals, logging, and failure paths. The session is vendor-neutral and focused on immediate decisions: what to automate, what to keep human, and how to determine whether the workflow is actually useful.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio: Marcus Rosser is a New Orleans–based creative technologist, educator, and founder of RT Solutions and Roser Gallery. Through RT Solutions, he develops practical AI workflows, automation systems, and hands-on learning programs for small businesses, educators, artists, nonprofits, and public-sector partners. A Security+ certified former IT manager, he also leads university-affiliated youth technology programs with LSU and UNO. His work connects responsible technology, creative practice, and community ownership.

title.rendered: Open the Studio: A Community Technology Curriculum Anyone Can Run by Marcus Rosser

content.rendered: Community technology programs often disappear when the expert, equipment, or grant leaves. Marcus Rosser presents an open-source program kit developed from New Orleans gallery workshops and university-affiliated youth programs: facilitator guides, project briefs, equipment-light alternatives, safety and privacy checklists, assessment tools, and reusable AI and 3D-printing activities. Attendees will see how to turn a one-time workshop into a maintainable program that a teacher, artist, library, or nonprofit can run, adapt, and improve.

title.rendered: Beyond Technical Expertise: The Skills That Drive Success by Nathan Stockman

content.rendered: Technical expertise may open the door, but transferable skills—such as communication, collaboration, adaptability, problem-solving, and self-management—determine how people navigate change, contribute to teams, and grow into leadership. In this interactive session, participants will define soft skills, compare their perceptions with the most in-demand skills across industries, and explore how technical and transferable skills develop along different trajectories. Participants will also examine practical ways mentorship, feedback, reflection, and intentional practice can strengthen these skills in technical workplaces.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio: Nathan leads YouthForce NOLA’s work to improve soft skills development and industry based credential attainment of students in New Orleans public high schools. His role as Chief of Education and Training Partnerships requires him to lead a team that works with all NOLA PS open enrollment schools to improve Career Connected Learning outcomes. Nathan joined YouthForce in 2020 as Director of Learning Design, working almost exclusively on soft skills. In his prior role as principal of Einstein Charter High School, Nathan established a foundation of academic growth spurred by belief in the strong connection between career technical education and core subject areas. His Einstein students experienced success striving for industry-based credentials, which paid dividends when taking LEAP, CLEP, and AP exams. Originally from Toronto, Ontario, Nathan holds a master’s in Secondary Education and an undergraduate degree in English from the University of Montevallo in  Alabama. Nathan and his wife have two daughters.

title.rendered: Why machines cannot crochet by Julia Feliciano

content.rendered:
Only human hands can crochet, and that is one of the most interesting facts in textile history.

Unlike knitting, which has been successfully mechanized since the 16th century, crochet has resisted automation for structural reasons. Its unique combination of tension and loop sequences makes it much harder to replicate mechanically.

Historians cannot agree on the exact origin of crochet, but some recent neuroscience studies suggest that this technique reduces the odds of developing cognitive impairment and triggers a physiological relaxation response. Artists of all genders have been reclaiming crochet as a material source of expression, challenging the hierarchy between art and craft in repressive domesticity.

There are many ways we can frame and practice this 200-year-old textile technique, from artistic expression to anti-brain-rot exercise, and all of them can be started from a group of four basic stitches that can only be performed by human hands and will be taught in this workshop.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
Julia is a Brazilian professional based in New Orleans since 2025. 

She brings 4 years of experience in SaaS Product Management and Customer Success. As well as 8 years of project management experience, coordinating stakeholders, timelines, and goals. She draws on expertise from outside of tech to ask sharper questions and to translate requirements across multiple stakeholders to maintain a coherent product vision. 

Her career has been a multidisciplinary web connecting people, priorities, and resources to move initiatives forward in complex organizations. 

Her current interests are also multidisciplinary: AI safety and governance, invisible history, crafts as art, and human-centered innovation.

title.rendered: Entrepreneurs’ Tarot: A Strategic Mirror by Greg Bresnitz

content.rendered: Founders have more analytical tools than any generation in history and still can’t answer the questions that matter: should I take this money, fire this person, kill this product? Entrepreneurs’ Tarot uses a 600-year-old deck of 22 archetypes as pattern recognition for exactly those decisions. No fortune telling, no algorithm, no screen. Greg has pulled cards for founders, investors, and C-suite executives at conferences worldwide, and he’ll show the room how a stack of paper still outperforms a dashboard when the question is human. Live pull included.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio: Greg Bresnitz is a multiple-time founder and former CEO of a top-tier VC-backed company who spent two decades inside the rooms where these decisions get made. He now runs Entrepreneurs’ Tarot, a strategic mirror for founders: private readings, live event activations, and a weekly readings column followed by thousands of founders, executives, and investors. He has read for leaders at FWB Fest, Tulane’s Freeman School, Nieux Society, and conferences worldwide. He lives in New Orleans. entrepreneurstarot.com

title.rendered: Nobody Asked for This by Cam’ron Caldwell

content.rendered:
Who’s it for? What’s the point? Hasn’t someone done this already?

Maybe we’re asking too many questions too early. “Nobody Asked for This” is about treating technology as a creative medium, following curiosity, making weird things, and figuring out the “why” later.

Get creative. Get weird. Get going.

title.rendered: “Who you Callin’ soft?!” People skills and Communication skills in the agentic age. by Stefan Poole

content.rendered: This presentation will take a close look at talents that, in another time, would be phased out of a one-page resume to make room for tech-specific proficiencies and experiences. Communication, mediation, street smarts, even philosophy and diction are far more important than they were less than 5 years ago. This presentation will discuss which of these “soft skills” are most beneficial for creating, prompting, guiding, and leveraging your agents for better outcomes per outcome. Less “Computer Science”, more “Computer Philosophy”.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio: Stephen Poole is a New Orleans engineer who builds agentic tooling, workflow automation, and the occasional rescued WordPress site. He’s shipped Claude skills, and an n8n immigration intake automation built alongside Union Migrante volunteers. He has walked a non-profit board through  payment platform options, trained box office staff through a full ticketing system migration, and fronted a fifteen-piece Afrobeat orchestra for crowds of 5,000. He’s found the things that are most important for building a system have a lot to do with the most important things for building a team.

title.rendered: Analog Intelligence Since 1440: A Hands-On Letterpress Workshop by Joseph Makkos

content.rendered:
Nearly six centuries before artificial intelligence, movable type transformed how humans created, organized, and shared information. Analog Intelligence Since 1440 invites participants to step away from the screen and experience this revolutionary technology firsthand.

In this 90-minute hands-on workshop, participants will work with movable type, spacing, ornaments, ink, and a working letterpress to explore the fundamentals of traditional typographic design. Together, we’ll compose and print using the same basic system that has shaped printed communication for centuries: individual pieces of type assembled by hand, locked into place, inked, and pressed onto paper.

Along the way, we’ll consider what this deeply physical process can teach us in an age of generative tools: constraint, intentionality, material knowledge, and the relationship between human decisions and the technologies we use to make things. Participants will leave with a letterpress print and a firsthand understanding of one of history’s most consequential information technologies.

title.rendered: Small Language Models: The Most Important, Least Understood, Highly Impactful Portion of the Industry by Sabelo Jupiter

content.rendered: Small language models — ordinary transformers, could be from 100M to 50B parameters, maybe more maybe less — now match systems ten times their size from a year ago in performance. Some are even trained small from scratch, something we didn’t think was possible. This talk covers where SLMs came from (a decade of discovering that models are mostly compressible air, from AlexNet to BitNet), the current state of the art, and, most importantly, why they matter to you: anyone can train and own one, they run entirely on an 8 GB laptop or phone — your data never leaves your machine — they use a fraction of the energy, and they’re a hedge against rising AI prices. Rent intelligence, or own it.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
I am a Machine Learning Engineer and Data Scientist with proven success delivering high-value analytics and generative AI solutions for government and enterprise. I’ve worked on projects causing $1B+ in fraud prevention savings for the US Treasury and enhanced real-time data systems for rapid decision-making.

I specialize in building robust ML pipelines, deploying classical and deep learning models (NLP, computer vision, entity resolution), and optimizing data flows in cloud environments (AWS Lambda, Redshift, Docker, Step Functions). A core focus of my recent work is small language models (SLMs) — fine-tuning, distilling, and quantizing compact models to deliver LLM-quality results at a fraction of the cost, latency, and infrastructure footprint, including deployments in resource-constrained and privacy-sensitive environments where large hosted models aren’t an option. I thrive when translating complex technical concepts for diverse stakeholders, driving impact across cross-functional teams.

My experience spans computer science, applied mathematics, and cross-industry data applications, including leading conference talks and collaborating on AI community events. As a lifelong learner, I am passionate about pairing technical expertise with clear communication to unlock transformative solutions.

Ask me about designing scalable ML architecture, small language models and efficient AI, tackling data-intensive projects, or speaking on generative AI trends.

title.rendered: AI is changing marketing by William Dalton

content.rendered:
AI is most powerful when it doesn’t replace what you’re good at… it helps you do your magic better. In this session, Bill Dalton will demonstrate how he combines decades of marketing experience with AI to work faster, dig deeper, ask better questions and uncover opportunities that would have previously required far more time and effort.

Using real-world marketing and market research examples, Bill will show how your own expertise, instincts and judgment can become the fuel that makes AI dramatically more useful. The goal isn’t to hand your job over to AI. It’s to discover how AI can amplify what you already know and help you become better at what you do.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
Bill Dalton describes himself as a business and marketing nerd… someone who genuinely enjoys figuring out how businesses work, grow and find new opportunities. Raised in New Orleans, he attended the University of Louisiana at Lafayette as a proud Ragin’ Cajun and started his first businesses there, including providing slide-imaging services for presentations… technology some people in the audience may now need to Google.

Bill has worked in advertising and marketing since 1994 and is the founder and CEO of Louisiana-based Firefly Marketing Solutions. After 15 years in Lafayette, he returned to New Orleans in 2004 and expanded Firefly’s reach across South Louisiana, with particular experience in the energy, maritime and government sectors. Throughout that growth, his philosophy has remained simple: strong relationships get you in the door, while great relationships and technical expertise keep clients and help both businesses grow.

Within weeks of ChatGPT’s release in late 2022, Bill recognized that AI would fundamentally change how people research, learn and apply their expertise. Today, ChatGPT, Claude and Perplexity are part of his daily workflow. He regularly speaks with business groups about AI and productivity, with a particular focus on helping people use AI to amplify the knowledge, experience and skills they already possess.

And when he isn’t obsessing over business, marketing or AI, Bill and his family live four blocks from the Sauvage Street entrance to Jazz Fest, where hosting pre- and post-Fest gatherings every day has become an annual tradition.

title.rendered: We’re Building Computers in a Garage Again by Rob Gaudet

content.rendered:
Every business running AI today is stacking parts, not building systems — swapping models, duct-taping prompts, re-explaining themselves to a chatbot with no memory. That’s the hardware era. Steve Jobs and Woz in the garage, before there was an OS.

This talk makes the case that context is the missing operating system layer — the thing that sits between the raw model (the hardware, a fast-commoditizing chip anyone can swap) and the apps and agents everyone’s racing to build on top. Without it, every “AI app” is just another peripheral with no memory of what it’s plugged into.

We’ll cover: why LLMs are becoming interchangeable, why “prompting” is already obsolete, what a real context layer looks like, and what businesses should be building now — before the OS layer gets built by someone else, for them.

20 minutes, or a full half-day workshop where we build a first context layer live.

scraped_fields.presenter_bio:
Hi! My name is Rob Gaudet. I architect agentic AI systems and ship them solo. Then I build the audience that finds them.

Victora.ai is the flagship. Multi-tenant SaaS running autonomous Claude workflows on Cloudflare Workers and Supabase Postgres, with a database-driven task engine, multi-model routing between Sonnet and Haiku, and structured context that persists across every run. No team. Just me, Claude Code, and a locked shipping sequence.

The same stack drives everything else I run. AuntMabel.app puts an AI voice agent on the phone with seniors living alone every morning. InkThorn.ai and TrustLight.com take the same agent architecture into publishing and into South Louisiana trades. Gaudet Systems is where I do the architecture work for everyone else.

Distribution is the other half of the job. I’ve built a 220,000-follower community that reaches 60 million people a year and funds $1M annually in disaster relief. I’ve spent $250K on Facebook ads and returned over $6 million. In 2012, before Facebook Marketplace existed, I built 130 city-level buy-sell-trade groups by reverse-engineering what people actually type into search. They now hold 3 million members and I never ran an ad. In 2009 I built my first 500,000-person following from zero.

I’ve been early before. In 2006 Microsoft brought me to Redmond to co-write the .NET Architecture certification exams. In 2012 I built LILAH, an FDA-cleared remote patient monitoring platform, before telehealth was a word. That architecture is standard across the industry now. It sold for $300 million.

30 years of production software. The last three have been the most interesting ones.
